clue.text: A stronghold of speed

explanation.surface: A fortress described as a seat of speed.
explanation.definitionFit: A fastness is a secure fortified retreat, and also the quality of being quick, rapidity.

clue.text: Omen of bird gone wild

indicators.note: something gone wild is out of control, so the letters are thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: A bird flying out of control taken as a bad sign.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wild' rearranges OF, BIRD and GONE.
explanation.definitionFit: A foreboding is a premonition of evil, so it works as a portent.

clue.text: Whereby those making sallies may fog the issue

definitions.text: Whereby those making sallies may fog the issue

parts.words: Whereby those making sallies may fog the issue
parts.note: sallies are witty remarks but also sorties by troops, who throw a device to create a screen of fog

explanation.surface: How people making witticisms can confuse an argument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sallies' are military sorties as well as quips, and 'fog the issue' is literal: a device thrown to cover an advance with a screen.
explanation.definitionFit: A canister that produces a dense cloud to hide troops from the enemy.

clue.text: Famous, as a song

explanation.surface: Well known, like a popular tune.
explanation.walkthrough: A song is written in musical notes, so it is 'note-d'.
explanation.definitionFit: Well-known people are renowned; and a tune set out in musical symbols is written in notes.

clue.text: Seasonal financial differences would be useless to 9

definitions.text: Seasonal financial differences would be useless to 9

parts.words: Seasonal financial differences would be useless to 9
parts.note: the season after winter plus the gaps between debit and credit gives weighing devices, useless where nothing weighs anything

explanation.surface: Gaps in accounts that come round each year are no help to an astronaut.
explanation.walkthrough: SPRING (a season) + BALANCES (financial differences) gives a weighing device that works by a coiled metal piece; to the 9-down space traveller, weightless, it reads zero.
explanation.definitionFit: A weighing instrument using a coil's stretch, pointless without gravity.

clue.text: Soulful girl

parts.note: the maiden of Greek myth loved by Cupid, whose name is also the Greek word for the soul or spirit

explanation.surface: A description of a deeply emotional young woman.
explanation.definitionFit: In myth she is the mortal girl Cupid loved, and the word also means the human soul or mind.

clue.text: Over-trained officer reaches deadlock

parts.note: an athlete who has trained too much is said to have gone stale
a mate is a merchant ship's officer

explanation.surface: A worn-out officer gets stuck at an impasse.
explanation.walkthrough: In chess this is the position where the player to move has no legal move, so the game is drawn.
explanation.definitionFit: A situation where neither side can make progress is an impasse.

clue.text: Calls on a hundred to rise in disorder

indicators.note: in a down clue one piece placed on another comes before it

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred

indicators.note: letters in disorder are jumbled into a new sequence

explanation.surface: A summons to a hundred people to rise up in a riot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in disorder' rearranges RISE into RIES, placed under C.
explanation.definitionFit: Shouts or calls out are yells.

clue.text: Good Queen Bess has general service work units

parts.note: Elizabeth I, whose royal cipher is ER, Elizabeth Regina
GS is the abbreviation for general service

explanation.surface: Queen Elizabeth I possessing army general service work units.
explanation.walkthrough: ER is Elizabeth Regina, used for any Queen Elizabeth.
explanation.definitionFit: An erg is a small unit of energy, the work done in the old centimetre-gram-second system.

clue.text: His journey gives rise to no weighty problems

definitions.text: His journey gives rise to no weighty problems

parts.words: His journey gives rise to no weighty problems
parts.note: a voyager beyond Earth floats free of gravity, so nothing he carries has any weight

explanation.surface: Someone whose trip causes no serious trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gives rise' is literal lift-off, and 'no weighty problems' is weightlessness, not a lack of serious difficulties.
explanation.definitionFit: An astronaut journeys beyond the atmosphere, where things become weightless.

clue.text: To which one's foul deeds come home ? Sound idea

definitions.text: To which one's foul deeds come home ? Sound idea

parts.words: To which one's foul deeds come home ? Sound idea
parts.note: curses, like chickens, come home to perch at night; 'foul' sounds like 'fowl', so the deeds are birds returning to their perch

explanation.surface: A moralising remark that misdeeds always return to the doer, called a sound thought.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb says curses come home to roost; 'Sound idea' tells you to hear 'foul' as 'fowl', birds that come home at dusk to their perch.
explanation.definitionFit: A perch where birds settle for the night is where wrongdoing proverbially returns.

clue.text: Finding a substitute for one? Could mean a setback

explanation.surface: Someone looking for a stand-in, worried it might be a reverse.
explanation.walkthrough: Split it as RE-PLACING: placing something back again, which is literally setting it back.
explanation.definitionFit: Finding a substitute is putting another in someone's stead; read as re-placing it means putting something back where it was.

clue.text: " Bachelor's fare ;——, and kisses " (Swift)

parts.note: a line of Jonathan Swift's with a gap to fill: a bachelor's simple meal named before the kisses

explanation.surface: A quotation from Swift about what a single man lives on.
explanation.walkthrough: This is a fill-in-the-blank quotation: Swift wrote of a bachelor's fare as a plain meal of the staples, plus kisses.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names the plainest of meals, the loaf and the cheese a single man would eat.

clue.text: " Respectable —— of the Dismal Science " (Carlyle)

parts.note: Carlyle called economics the dismal science; the gap is the academics who teach it

explanation.surface: A quotation from Thomas Carlyle about economics.
explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in-the-blank quotation: Thomas Carlyle wrote of the 'Respectable Professors of the Dismal Science', his name for economics.
explanation.definitionFit: The holders of university chairs, here in economics, are its senior academics.

clue.text: Make a contribution to Lorna's portion

explanation.surface: Helping out by giving a share to a woman called Lorna.
explanation.walkthrough: Lorna Doone is the heroine of R. D. Blackmore's novel, so Lorna's portion is Doone's bit, read as a phrase meaning to play your part.
explanation.definitionFit: To play one's part is to help out; and the heroine's surname plus a share gives her portion.

clue.text: Including the substance in East China

indicators.note: the substance goes inside the word for China

parts.note: the Ming dynasty ruled China, and Ming is used for Chinese porcelain
the body is the main substance of something

explanation.surface: Containing material found in eastern China.
explanation.walkthrough: 'China' suggests a country, but here it is the dynasty whose name stands for Chinese porcelain; 'in' signals the container.
explanation.definitionFit: To embody something is to include it as part of a whole.

clue.text: Fill me in about a' backward Eastern potentate

indicators.note: 'Fill me in' says the word me is put inside the letters that follow
the letters for about and a are read from the end, giving the outer piece

parts.note: re is Latin for about, concerning
taken as written

explanation.surface: A request to brief someone on an Eastern ruler who is behind the times.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backward' turns about-plus-a into AER; 'Fill me in' then signals the insertion. 'backward' looks like a dig at the potentate.
explanation.definitionFit: An ameer, or emir, is a Muslim ruler or commander in the East.

clue.text: Careful manager for a periodical

explanation.surface: A thrifty manager working for a magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: The Economist is a British weekly news magazine.
explanation.definitionFit: A thrifty person manages money sparingly; and the London weekly news magazine bears that name.

clue.text: Pile-maker in India

parts.note: a pile is a fortune; the clue suggests a builder or weaver but means a man who grew rich in India

explanation.surface: Someone who builds stacks or weaves carpet pile in India.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pile' means a fortune: the word was used for Britons who came home from India very rich.
explanation.definitionFit: The term was used for a European who made a large fortune in India, from a title of a provincial governor.

clue.text: Stops to bring back nudity in Eden

definitions.text: to bring back nudity in Eden

explanation.surface: Halting the return of nakedness to the Garden of Eden.
explanation.walkthrough: Adam and Eve covered themselves with fig leaves, so to take the leaves off would make them naked again.
explanation.definitionFit: To cease doing something is to quit; and removing the fig foliage would return Eden to nakedness.

clue.text: Stepping stones for crossing the Styx ?

definitions.text: Stepping stones for crossing the Styx ?

parts.words: Stepping stones for crossing the Styx ?
parts.note: the Styx is the river bordering the underworld, and the proverbial road to hell is paved with well-meant plans

explanation.surface: A question about how to walk across the river to the underworld.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'the road to hell is paved with good intentions' turns into stones laid across the Styx, the river of the Greek underworld.
explanation.definitionFit: Well-meant plans that never happen proverbially pave the way to hell.

clue.text: Happen to be a dog-handler

explanation.surface: Someone who happens to work with dogs.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the second part as OC CUR: an Officer Commanding a cur, someone in charge of a dog.
explanation.definitionFit: Things that come about take place; and an officer commanding a mongrel is one in charge of a dog.

clue.text: Abstract party role in Alpine region

indicators.note: to abstract is to draw out, so the letters are drawn from inside the words party role

explanation.surface: A political role, described as abstract, in a mountain district.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Abstract' looks like an adjective for the role but tells you to draw letters out of 'party role'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tyrol is a mountain area of the Alps in Austria and Italy.

clue.text: Far from the cream of the population, though floating

definitions.text: Far from the cream of the population, though floating

parts.words: Far from the cream of the population, though floating
parts.note: the lowest of society, yet like a froth it rises to the top of a liquid as cream does

explanation.surface: A remark about the lowest class who drift about.
explanation.walkthrough: Cream floats on milk; this also floats, but it is the worst of people rather than the best.
explanation.definitionFit: Froth on a liquid's top is also a contemptuous word for worthless people.

clue.text: It's colourful fuel we get out of the valley

indicators.note: the fuel word stands outside the valley word, wrapping round it

parts.note: coal is a fuel
a chine is a deep narrow ravine, a word used in Dorset and the Isle of Wight

explanation.surface: A bright thing we extract from fuel found down in the valley.
explanation.walkthrough: 'we get out of' looks like extraction, but it means the fuel sits outside, wrapping the valley word. A chine is a steep ravine on the English south coast.
explanation.definitionFit: Cochineal is a red dye made from crushed insects, so it gives colour.

clue.text: Pachydermatous wealth

explanation.surface: Thick-skinned riches, a picture of a callous rich man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rhino' is old British slang for money.
explanation.definitionFit: The thick-skinned beast is a pachyderm, and old slang uses the word for cash.

clue.text: Illusion of anger on the road

indicators.note: in a down-or-across charade, on says one piece is put next to the other, here after it

parts.note: the M1 is Britain's main motorway, written with a 1 that looks like the letter I
rage is anger

explanation.surface: A false impression caused by temper on the highway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'anger on the road' suggests road rage; the M1, London to Leeds motorway, is read as MI with the numeral as an I.
explanation.definitionFit: A mirage is an optical illusion, such as water seen on a hot road.

clue.text: Have reference, in an afterthought, to ecclesiastics

indicators.note: the words for having reference go inside the afterthought

parts.note: a postscript, PS, is an afterthought added to a letter
to relate to something is to have reference to it

explanation.surface: Mentioning churchmen only as an afterthought in a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Prelates are senior churchmen such as bishops.
